summary.text: Anglerfish are ray-finned fish of the order Lophiiformes, named for a modified fin ray on the back that acts as a lure for prey.
They live in seas worldwide, from tropical to polar waters, with many species resting on the seabed and the deep-sea kinds drifting in open water.
In deep-sea anglerfish, males attach to the much larger females and sometimes fuse with them, a habit known as sexual parasitism.

facts.label: Parts of the lure
facts.value: Esca at the tip, illicium along the length

facts.label: Largest member
facts.value: European monkfish, up to 200 cm long

facts.label: Earliest fossils
facts.value: Eocene, from Monte Bolca in Italy

facts.label: Sold as food
facts.value: As monkfish or goosefish, valued as a delicacy

paragraphs.heading: A fish that goes fishing
paragraphs.text: Anglerfish are a group of ray-finned fish that make up the order Lophiiformes. Their name comes from how they hunt. One spine of the fin on their back has turned into a lure, a little like an angler's rod and bait, that draws prey in. The tip of this lure is called the esca and its stalk the illicium, and each species shapes and works it to tempt particular kinds of prey.

paragraphs.heading: From reefs to the deep
paragraphs.text: Anglerfish live in seas all over the world, from tropical waters to the polar regions, and from shallow coasts down to the deep sea. Many kinds, such as monkfishes, batfishes, frogfishes and sea toads, live on or near the bottom and use enlarged fins to rest on the seabed or creep across it. Frogfishes are usually short and crawl or perch among reef life on fins that work like limbs. The deep-sea anglerfish are different: they have no pelvic fins, they drift and swim in open water, and they are usually weak swimmers.

paragraphs.heading: Waiting for a meal
paragraphs.text: Anglerfish generally hunt by ambush. Shallow-water kinds such as frogfish often disguise themselves as rocks, sponges or seaweed. In the deep sea, anglerfish are grey to brown, so they blend into the dark water around them. In most species a wide mouth wraps around the front of the head, and both jaws carry bands of teeth that slope inward. The teeth can fold back, so prey slides easily toward the stomach but cannot get out again.

paragraphs.heading: Huge females, tiny males
paragraphs.text: Male and female anglerfish can differ hugely, a difference called sexual dimorphism. In some species the female is several orders of magnitude heavier than the male. In the deep-sea warty anglerfish, males reach up to 16 cm while females are commonly around 77 cm long. In deep-sea anglerfish this gap made an odd way of breeding possible: the male attaches to the far bigger female and sometimes fuses with her body, a habit known as sexual parasitism. Mature males of one species, Photocorynus spiniceps, are only 6.2 to 7.3 mm long and were once claimed as the smallest known vertebrate, but because they do not live freely they are now often left out of the records.

paragraphs.heading: Small fish and giants
paragraphs.text: Anglerfish range from about 2 to 18 cm long, with a few species growing past 100 cm. The biggest is the European monkfish, which can reach 200 cm and 57.7 kg. In monkfish the sexes are much closer in size than in the deep-sea kinds, so the size gap is not extreme in every group.

paragraphs.heading: On the plate and in the rocks
paragraphs.text: Anglerfish matter to people too. Many species are of interest to aquariums, and the lophiid anglerfish, sold as monkfish, goosefish or simply angler, are caught commercially because their meat is prized as a delicacy around the world. The oldest anglerfish fossils come from the Eocene rocks of Monte Bolca in Italy, and they already show the group splitting into its modern families. That, together with their close kinship to the Tetraodontiformes, which are known from Cretaceous fossils, suggests anglerfish probably arose in the Cretaceous.
